title: Mercy and compassion
description: Five passages that take mercy seriously in different registers. Read them as distinct claims, not as a single universal ethic. The notes identify what each passage is doing in its own tradition.

items.annotation: A beatitude: mercy is both a practice and a promise. The Greek ἐλεήμων is closer to 'merciful' than to a general benevolence.
The basmala names God as al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm. The two names share a root but are not simply synonyms in traditional commentary.
Hatred is ended by love (mettā), not by more hatred. The claim is about a causal cycle, not a command issued by a deity.
חֶסֶד (chesed) is often translated 'mercy' or 'steadfast love'. It carries covenantal overtones that 'mercy' alone may obscure.
Jain non-violence begins with attention to the harm one causes other living beings. The scope and rationale differ from the other passages.

title: The examined life
description: What does it mean to examine one's life, and what does such examination demand? These passages range from Socratic defiance to Chinese learning, Buddhist attention and Daoist reticence.

items.annotation: Socrates refuses to abandon public questioning even to avoid death. The passage is Plato's literary reconstruction, not a transcript.
Marcus begins Book II with a morning exercise in attention to his own judgements and to mortality.
Learning is practised, shared and sustained without recognition. The Confucian examined life is relational and ritual.
The examination is of intention and its consequences. The Pali term manopubbaṅgamā places mind at the head of ethical experience.
The Daodejing cautions that the Way cannot be captured in speech. Its 'examination' is a discipline of not grasping.

title: Duty without grasping
description: Four accounts of action that do not cling to results. The similarities are real but partial; the underlying metaphysics and ethical goals are not interchangeable.

items.annotation: Krishna instructs Arjuna to act without attachment to the fruits of action and to cultivate equanimity. The verses belong to a longer argument about self, duty and devotion.
The sage gives without accumulating and acts without contending. The frame is the Way, not a divine commander.
Confucian seriousness about learning and fault-correction is a discipline of character, not a theory of detachment from results.
Stoic practice redirects attention from outcomes to the quality of one's own judgements and actions.

title: Mortality and the span of life
description: Death is approached as threat, teacher, transition and natural process. The comparison is designed to show disagreement, not to manufacture a common consolation.

items.annotation: The speaker walks through the valley of the shadow of death and speaks of accompaniment rather than escape.
Life is a point, a stream and a pilgrimage. Philosophy is what can be carried through it.
God is the Living and Eternal; the verse contrasts divine self-subsistence with the dependence of all else.
Socrates does not claim to know what death is, but refuses to purchase survival by abandoning the examined life.

title: Naming and remembering
description: Five passages on the name of the divine: asserted as truth, remembered as a practice, spoken as a Word, and withheld from language altogether. The positions are not versions of one doctrine; they disagree about what a name can do.

items.annotation: The Mūl Mantar, which stands at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib and opens the Japjī. 'The Name is truth' (sati nāmu) treats the Name as a description of what is real rather than a label attached to it; ੴ (ik onkār) is written as a single glyph. The English is Sant Singh Khalsa's 2003 rendering, used with written permission from the rights holders.

Also from the Japjī: thought cannot bring the divine within the reach of thought, however much thinking is done. The line is apophatic in force, yet it sits inside a hymn that has just named the One, so negation and affirmation belong to the same utterance.
Remembrance (dhikr) is a practice, and the verse names its effect: hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Pickthall's 1930 translation; the Arabic is shown in the parallel edition.
The prologue of John identifies the Logos with God, so the Word is not a name for God but God. Greek λόγος carries speech, reason and account together, which no single English word reproduces.

The Daodejing opens by withholding what the other passages grant: a way that can be trodden and a name that can be named are not the enduring ones. Legge leaves 'Tao' untranslated; the Chinese is shown in the parallel edition.
